en: Amṛtaprabhāsādhanopāyikā by Ḍombīheruka = Matsunaga 307 IV = Sādhanamālā 228.
= Readings reported by the editor, p. 443.
[20r] Oṃ, homage to Nairātmyā!
The meditation on the wheel of goddesses was taught by the venerable Ḍombīheruka,
having condensed the entire reality from the *Hevajra-yoginī-tantra*. Having beheld the Lord, the Master, the Sovereign of the Vajra, in the sky...
The wise one should worship and pay homage to the reflected image of Akṣobhya.
Having meditated upon his own seed-syllable in the heart, he should fashion a cloud of offerings,
constantly employing the five nectars together with the eight Mothers.
The five yoginīs beginning with Gaurī are considered to be the bearers of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
along with Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī, through their embrace of the vessel of flavors.
One should constantly offer the water of honor (argha) and likewise rejoice in merit.
They go for refuge to the Three Jewels and maintain the thought of enlightenment.
First, having meditated on loving-kindness, one should subsequently cultivate compassion.
Again, having meditated on sympathetic joy (*muditā*), one should then contemplate equanimity (*upekṣā*) in its entirety.
Following that, one should recite the mantras of the Victors:
*Oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.
Having meditated upon oneself and others as empty, the yogi should recollect his vow.
Having visualized the sun in front by means of the syllable *repha*, he should visualize a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) arising from the syllable *hūṃ* within that sun.
And with that very same vajra, one should visualize a rampart and a cage-binding.
The wise one should contemplate within the element of space Prajñā in the form of the syllable *e*;
therein he should visualize the earth as square and greenish-yellow.
One should visualize the water-maṇḍala situated in the center of the earth-maṇḍala;
one should then place fire within the waters, and the wind-maṇḍala within the fire.
Then, one should contemplate oneself situated in the center of the mandala of wind;
having become unified, the wheel becomes of a single form with the self.
It is quadrangular with four gates, adorned with eight pillars,
provided with necklaces and half-necklaces, and decorated with vajra-lines.
On that wheel, one should contemplate fifteen [beings] whose life-force has departed;
from the direction of the Yoginī, the fifteenth is considered the seat.
Upon the seat, one should place the moon, and upon the moon, the sun;
between these two, one should install the seed-syllable beginning with the root vowel.
The mirror-like wisdom and the wisdom of equality are proclaimed as the sun and the moon; the sword arising from the syllable AṂ is said to be the wisdom of discernment.
The unity of these is their performance, their accomplishment, and their pure nature;
the body of the Yoginīs is proclaimed to consist of the five gnoses.
And likewise, when the water has become variegated by the moon, the sun, and the crescent,
and has subsequently become mixed together, she should be known as the Yoginī Nairātmyā.
She is black in color, most terrible, and adorned with the five mudrās; in her right hand she holds a most fearsome flaying knife, and in her left a lotus vessel;
in her left [other] hand she holds a vajra-khaṭvāṅga, and she is girt at the waist with a tiger skin.
A, ā, i, ī, and u are said to belong to Nairātmyā and the others;
u, ṛ, ṝ, and ḷ are declared to belong to Pukkasī and the others;
and ḹ, e, ai, and o are the seed-syllables of Gaurī and the others.
The seed-syllables *au*, *aṃ*, and *bī* are again stated for her who dwells below and above.
One should seal Nairātmyā and the others, who are situated within the enclosure of Wisdom, with Citta, Śāśvata, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi;
[likewise] with the Tathāgatas Citta, Śāśvata, Ratneśa, and Amitāyus.
One should seal the Pukkasī and others situated in the intermediate directions in the direct order.
But the sealing of the four Yoginīs who always abide at the gates is performed by means of the vajras of hatred, delusion, envy, and passion.
One should perform the sealing of body and speech, being composed in the upper and lower [parts];
it is called "sealing" because one is sealed by means of a characteristic mark.
In the east is Vajrā, in the south Gaurī, in the west Vāriyoginī,
in the north Vajraḍākinī, and in the center Nairātmyayoginī.
In the northeast, Pukkasī is renowned; likewise, Śabarī is in the southeast;
Caṇḍālī is in the direction of the Rākṣasas (the southwest); and likewise, Ḍombinī is in the northwest.
Furthermore, at the eastern gate is Gaurī; likewise, Caurikā is at the southern [gate];
Vetālī is at the western gate; and likewise, Ghasmarī is at the northern [gate].
The Bhūcarī is known to be below, and the Khecarī is remembered as being above;
all of them bestow supreme bliss, just like the Yoginī Nairātmyā.
Having meditated on one's own seed-syllable in the heart, one should then emit rays of light;
having drawn in the Perfect Buddhas by means of those rays, one should worship them with the eight Mothers.
Thereafter, one should offer a supplication to the Blessed Great Beings:
"May the Blessed Ones, all the Tathāgatas, grant me the state of empowerment."
Thereafter, the wise one is consecrated with jars filled with nectar;
while sprinkling [the disciple], he becomes Citteśa, crowned by all the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
One should first meditate on her as black; in the second [moment], one should visualize her as red;
in the third, one should meditate on her as yellow, and likewise in the fourth, as green.

In the fifth [stage], the yogi should meditate on her as having a blue complexion; in the sixth, with a very white body. He should meditate on her as possessing six limbs, and thereafter as being devoid of color.
Vajrā should be in the aggregate of form, Gaurī is remembered in sensation;
Vāriyoginī is in perception, and Vajraḍākinī is in mental formations.
Abiding in the form of the aggregate of consciousness, she is the Yoginī of Selflessness;
situated within the mandala, she is the Terrible One, who strikes fear even into fear itself.
Earth is known as Pukkasi, the water element is considered Śabarī;
fire should be known as Caṇḍālinī, and wind is proclaimed to be Ḍombī.
Gaurī is always renowned in the realm of form, and Caurī is proclaimed in the realm of sound;
Vetālī is in the sphere of smell, and likewise Ghasmarī is in the realm of taste.
Bhūcarī is known to be in touch, and Khecarī arises from the dharmadhātu;
for through the constant purification of the insubstantial, the yogins of reality attain accomplishment.
Mohavajrī is in the eyes, Dveṣavajrikā in the ears;
Mātsaryakī is said to be in the nose, and Rāgavajrikā in the mouth;
Sparśavajrī is in touch, and Nairātmyayoginī is in the mind.
With these, through great purification, for the sake of purifying the sense faculties,
[one attains] the ninth noble one, the clarified butter, the shaven-headed, and the deity-cutting knife.
He carries a skull, a defiled head, and eats upon the shoulder;
he wears a circlet for the purpose of bowing to his guru, preceptor, and chosen deity.
To prevent hearing ill-spoken words from one's guru or from Vajradhara,
earrings should be worn on the ears, and a necklace should be worn to recite the mantra.
Rucaka, having abandoned the slaughter of living beings, shall wear a girdle as a mudrā;
his body is always sealed with the thread of the five Buddhas.
The mantra: Oṃ a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ svāhā.
I shall now explain the purification of the measures (mātrā):
Akṣobhya is in the form of a wheel, and Amitābha is the nature of the earrings.
Ratneśa is said to be in the necklace around the neck, and Vairocana is in the hand.
Amogha is situated in Mekhalā; these five are the pure mothers.
They should be maintained by the yoginīs through the abandonment of faults, for they have always been held [by them].
I shall explain the internal form:
by means of the female form, one gains mastery over the world; by means of the wrathful form, one causes terror.
Through the union of the vowels and consonants, the external duality is practiced.
The mantra for agitating the city: *akacaṭatapayasa svāhā*.
The mantra for the bali offering to all spirits: *oṃ akāro mukhaṃ sarvadharmāṇām ādyam anutpannatvāt oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
I shall explain to you the vow of the Yoginī Nairātmyā;
she, the auspicious Mahāmudrā who produces great bliss, abides at the navel.
Because of her sharpness, she was enraged in the form of fire by the Mothers.
That wisdom, whose intrinsic nature is the primordial vowel, has been conceived by the Buddhas;
it remains pervading the three realms, yet it is not known by ordinary beings.
Abiding in the center of selflessness, the unstruck sound faces downward;
by means of the yoga of non-cessation, the bodhicitta flows forth perpetually.
Therefore, those channels within this body— the lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī—
have entered as the forms of body, speech, and mind, acting as artificial seals.
Lalanā is established as the nature of wisdom (prajñā), while rasanā exists as means (upāya);
avadhūtī, however, is in the central region, having the form of the support of great bliss (mahāsukha).
Lalanā brings about Akṣobhya, while Rasanā flows with blood;
Avadhūtī is always the foundational support of Amitanātha.
In the Sukhāvatī of the Karmamudrā, the three channels, according to their own time,
flow with body, speech, and mind, which are born from the Vajra-jewel.
The time for the urine of Vajra is said to be when [the deity] Ratnadhara appears in the form of the perfectly awakened Amitanātha while vomiting.
Knowledge always arises, whether spoken at the proper occasion or otherwise;
it is innate, supreme bliss, bringing happiness even to one's parents.
Just as someone, having lit a lamp within his house, eats during the night;
May there be happiness for those who seek [the truth], even with their bodies, as if by the darkness of delusion.

Having understood this ocean of existence— whose waters are poison, which is infested with crocodiles such as passion and the like, which is agitated by the waves of deep-rooted craving, and whose great shore is singular bliss—
why do people who possess the wisdom for enlightenment not strive, even for a moment, toward that which is solely intent upon their own true welfare?
They go to the further shore; having cast off the garment of the snare of delusion, they proceed to the marvelous.

The wise one should first perform the meditation on the generation stage; he must never forget the eternal armor consisting solely of the purification of the mudrās and mantras. Afterwards, endowed with excellence and with his mind one-pointedly focused on reality, the wise one should practice repeatedly.
One should always meditate upon this entire state arising from the cultivation of the generation stage.

He who wanders seated upon a tiger, adorned by various hooded serpents, who possesses great patience, and who dwells in the place known as Kaṅkageha— a place abounding in enjoyments and various sweets—
it was he, delighting in the welfare of others, who composed this sovereign sādhana involving the union of the secret and wisdom consorts.
O sons of the Conqueror, you should endure this which has been spoken by me, which illuminates the welfare of the world.
The ritual manual for the practice named Amṛtaprabhā is completed.
